messages.content: You are a helpful assistant that can interact with a computer.

Please solve this issue: We got our first GDPR erasure request, and it turns out Remove on the user
list doesn't remove anyone — it flips `active` off and scrambles the email,
and everything else stays.

Make it actually erase: nothing of theirs is left anywhere — not a row, not
a stale search hit. One exception: books they created that are shared with
everyone keep working — people are reading those. Take their name off and
byline them "Deleted author".

One wrinkle: most of the requests we owe are people someone already "removed"
the old way — deactivated, email rewritten to `alice-deactivated-<uuid>@...`.
It has to work for them too, and their sign-in log entries sit under the
address they actually signed in with.

--- README ---
# Writebook

### Instantly publish your own books on the web for free, no publisher required.

Writebook is an easy-to-use application for publishing content on the web.
Content is authored in Markdown, and books can contain picture pages, chapters, and title pages.
Books can be published privately or publicly, and are searchable.

## How to get Writebook

Writebook is distributed as a Docker image.
The simplest way to install and run it is by using [ONCE](https://github.com/basecamp/once).

To get started, paste this snippet into a terminal on the machine where you want to install Writebook:

```sh
curl https://get.once.com/writebook | sh
```

## Deploying manually with Docker

If you'd rather set the Docker image up yourself, you can use `docker run` or `docker compose` to do that.
The official image is `ghcr.io/basecamp/writebook`.

You'll need to route the incoming web traffic to ports 80 and 443 (or just 80 if you run without SSL).
To persist the storage of the application, mount a Docker volume to `/rails/storage`.

You can configure the SSL setting with the following environment variables:

- `SSL_DOMAIN` - enable automatic SSL via Let's Encrypt for the given domain name
- `DISABLE_SSL` - alternatively, set `DISABLE_SSL` to serve over plain HTTP

## Running in development

Install dependencies:

```sh
bin/setup
```

Start the development server:

```sh
bin/dev
```

module Book::Accessable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    has_many :accesses, dependent: :destroy
    scope :with_everyone_access, -> { where(everyone_access: true) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def accessable_or_published(user: Current.user)
      if user.present?
        accessable_or_published_books
      else
        published
      end
    end

    def accessable_or_published_books(user: Current.user)
      user.books.or(published).distinct
    end
  end

  def accessable?(user: Current.user)
    accesses.exists?(user: user)
  end

  def editable?(user: Current.user)
    access_for(user: user)&.editor? || user&.administrator?
  end

  def access_for(user: Current.user)
    accesses.find_by(user: user)
  end

  def update_access(editors:, readers:)
    editors = Set.new(editors)
    readers = Set.new(everyone_access? ? User.active.ids : readers)

    all = editors + readers
    all_accesses = all.collect { |user_id|
      { user_id: user_id, level: editors.include?(user_id) ? :editor : :reader }

class DemoContent
  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{
          (\[.+\])              # link title
          \(                    # opening paren
          \/\d+\/[\w-]+\/\d+\/  # leading portion of path
          ([\w-]+)              # leaf slug
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          link_title, leaf_slug, anchor = $1, $2, $3
          linked_page = pages[leaf_slug]
          raise "Invalid reference link: #{page_title}" unless linked_page.present?

          url = Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.leafable_slug_path(linked_page.leaf, anchor: anchor, only_path: true)

          "#{link_title}(#{url}"
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def with_attachment(filename)
        File.open(Rails.root.join("app/assets/images/demo/#{filename}")) do |file|
          yield io: file, filename: filename
        end
      end
  end
end

module Leaf::Searchable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  included do
    after_create_commit  :create_in_search_index,   if: :searchable?
    after_update_commit  :update_in_search_index,   if: :searchable?
    after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index, if: :searchable?

    scope :favoring_title, -> { order(Arel.sql("bm25(leaf_search_index, 2.0)")) }
  end

  class_methods do
    def reindex_all
      all.map &:reindex
    end

    def sanitize_query_syntax(terms)
      terms = terms.to_s
      terms = remove_invalid_search_characters(terms)
      terms = remove_unbalanced_quotes(terms)
      terms.presence
    end

    def search(terms)
      if terms = sanitize_query_syntax(terms)
        with_search_results_for(terms)
          .select(
            "leaves.*",
            "highlight(leaf_search_index, 0, '<mark>', '</mark>') as title_match",
            "snippet(leaf_search_index, 1, '<mark>', '</mark>', '...', 20) as content_match")
      else
        none
      end
    end

    def with_search_results_for(terms)
      joins("join leaf_search_index on leaves.id = leaf_search_index.rowid")
        .where("leaf_search_index match ?", terms)
    end
  end

  def reindex
    update_in_search_index if searchable?
  end

  def matches_for_highlight(terms)
    if terms = self.class.sanitize_query_syntax(terms)
      content = Leaf.with_search_results_for(terms)
        .where(id: id)
        .pick(Arel.sql("highlight(leaf_search_index, 1, '<mark>', '</mark>')"))

      content ? unique_matching_terms(content) : []
    end
  end

  private
    def searchable?
      searchable_content
    end

    # Strip tags from content before indexing to keep the FTS table clean.
    # This is a hygiene measure, not a security boundary — display-time
    # sanitization in sanitize_search_result is the primary defense.
    # ActionText content (Pages) is already HTML-safe plain text via
    # ERB::Util.html_escape, so skip it to avoid double-encoding.
    def sanitize_for_index(text)
      if text.html_safe?
        text
      else
        Rails::Html::FullSanitizer.new.sanitize(text)
      end
    end

    def create_in_search_index
      execute_sql_with_binds "insert into leaf_search_index(rowid, title, content ) values (?, ?, ?)",
        id, sanitize_for_index(title), sanitize_for_index(searchable_content)
    end

    def update_in_search_index
      transaction do
        updated = execute_sql_with_binds "update leaf_search_index set title = ?, content = ? where rowid = ?",
          sanitize_for_index(title), sanitize_for_index(searchable_content), id

        create_in_search_index unless updated
      end
    end

    def remove_from_search_index
      execute_sql_with_binds "delete from leaf_search_index where rowid = ?", id
    end

    def execute_sql_with_binds(*statement)
      self.class.connection.execute self.class.sanitize_sql(statement)

      self.class.connection.raw_connection.changes.nonzero?
    end

    def unique_matching_terms(content)
      terms = content.scan(/<mark>(.*?)<\/mark>/).flatten.uniq
      terms.sort_by(&:length).reverse
    end

    class_methods do
      private
        def remove_invalid_search_characters(terms)
          terms.gsub(/[^\w"]/, " ")
        end

        def remove_unbalanced_quotes(terms)
          if terms.count("\"").even?
            terms
          else
            terms.gsub("\"", " ")
          end
        end
    end
end

class DemoContent
  class << self
    def create_manual(user)
      book = create_book(user)
      load_markdown_pages(book)
    end

    private
      def create_book(user)
        Book.create(title: "The Writebook Manual", author: "37signals", everyone_access: true).tap do |book|
          with_attachment("writebook-manual.jpg") { |attachment| book.cover.attach(attachment) }
          book.update_access(readers: [], editors: [ user.id ])
        end
      end

      def load_markdown_pages(book)
        pages = {}

        Dir.glob(Rails.root.join("app/assets/markdown/demo/*.md")).each do |fname|
          front_matter = FrontMatterParser::Parser.parse_file(fname)

          if front_matter["class"] == "Section"
            load_section(book, front_matter)
          else
            page = load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
            attach_images(page)
            pages[page.leaf.slug] = page
          end
        end

        book.leaves.pages.each { |leaf| localize_ref_links(leaf.page, pages) }
      end

      def load_markdown_page(book, front_matter)
        book.press(Page.new(body: front_matter.content), title: front_matter["title"]).page
      end

      def load_section(book, front_matter)
        book.press Section.new(body: front_matter.content, theme: front_matter["theme"]), title: front_matter["title"]
      end

      def attach_images(page)
        re = %r{
          \/u\/           # leading portion of path
          (\S+-\w+\.\w+)  # filename including slug and extension
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          with_attachment($1) { |attachment| page.body.uploads.attach(attachment) }

          attachment = page.body.uploads.attachments.last
          attachment.analyze

          "/u/" + attachment.slug
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def localize_ref_links(page, pages)
        re = %r{
          (\[.+\])              # link title
          \(                    # opening paren
          \/\d+\/[\w-]+\/\d+\/  # leading portion of path
          ([\w-]+)              # leaf slug
        }x

        body = page.body.content.gsub(re) do |match|
          link_title, leaf_slug, anchor = $1, $2, $3
          linked_page = pages[leaf_slug]
          raise "Invalid reference link: #{page_title}" unless linked_page.present?

          url = Rails.application.routes.url_helpers.leafable_slug_path(linked_page.leaf, anchor: anchor, only_path: true)

          "#{link_title}(#{url}"
        end

        page.update!(body: body)
      end

      def with_attachment(filename)
        File.open(Rails.root.join("app/assets/images/demo/#{filename}")) do |file|
          yield io: file, filename: filename
        end
      end
  end
end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

module Leaf::Editable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

  MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS = 10.minutes

  included do
    has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all

    after_update :record_moved_to_trash, if: :was_trashed?
  end

  def edit(leafable_params: {}, leaf_params: {})
    if record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      update_and_record_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    else
      update_without_recording_edit leaf_params, leafable_params
    end
  end

  private
    def record_new_edit?(leafable_params)
      will_change_leafable?(leafable_params) && last_edit_old?
    end

    def last_edit_old?
      edits.empty? || edits.last.created_at.before?(MINIMUM_TIME_BETWEEN_VERSIONS.ago)
    end

    def will_change_leafable?(leafable_params)
      leafable_params.select do |key, value|
        leafable.attributes[key.to_s] != value
      end.present?
    end

    def update_without_recording_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.last&.touch
        update! leaf_params
      end
    end

    def update_and_record_edit(leaf_params, leafable_params)
      transaction do
        new_leafable = dup_leafable_with_attachments leafable
        new_leafable.update!(leafable_params)

        edits.revision.create!(leafable: leafable)
        update! leaf_params.merge(leafable: new_leafable)
      end
    end

    def dup_leafable_with_attachments(leafable)
      leafable.dup.tap do |new|
        leafable.attachment_reflections.each do |name, _|
          new.send(name).attach(leafable.send(name).blob)
        end
      end
    end

    def record_moved_to_trash
      edits.trash.create!(leafable: leafable)
    end

    def was_trashed?
      trashed? && previous_changes.include?(:status)
    end
end

messages.content: Let's run a diagnostic script in `bin/rails runner -e test` (cleaning up afterwards) to see every single leftover row across all tables when a book with covers, pages, uploads, pictures, sections, edits, trashed leaves, reading marks, accesses, and search index entries is destroyed!
messages.thinking:
**My Immediate Deep Dive into the `book.destroy!` Scenario**

Okay, hold on a minute! I need to *really* zoom in on the consequences of destroying a book, specifically when it's *not* set to be accessible to everyone. My mind is racing through every single related table and associated detail: `Book`, `Leaf`, `Edit`, `Page`, `Picture`, `Section`, `ActionText::Markdown`, `ActiveStorage`... everything. This destruction process has a lot of moving parts and possible side-effects.

My priority is to understand what happens to *all* the connected data when I call `book.destroy`. I need to precisely map what remains in the database *after* this happens. 

I'm thinking, let's start with a controlled environment. I'm going to set up a quick test in `bin/rails runner -e test` right now. 

I'm going to create a non-public book (`everyone_access: false`) and load it up with all sorts of related content, just to get a good sense of edge cases. I'll need to create:
1.  A book with a `cover` attachment using `ActiveStorage::Attachment`, `ActiveStorage::Blob` and the corresponding files in `storage/` for the assets.
2.  A `Page` with a populated `body` field (using `ActionText::Markdown`) AND an image attached to the page (using `page.body.uploads.attach(...)` leading to more `ActiveStorage::Attachment` and `ActiveStorage::Blob` entries.
3.  An `Edit` associated with that `Page` (created via `leaf.edit leafable_params: { body: "v2" }`).
4.  A `Picture` that has an `image` attachment and a variant (`ActiveStorage::VariantRecord`) and an associated `Edit`.
5.  A `Section` with some content in its `body` and a linked `Edit`.
6.  A "trashed" `Leaf` (`leaf.trashed!`, which should create a new `Edit` with an `:action` of `:trash` that points back to the same `leafable` as the original `Leaf`!).
7.  Some `ReadingMark` entries on leaves of that book.
8.  Some `Access` rows for that specific book.
9.  `leaf_search_index` entries tied to leaves that belong to that book!

Then, I'm going to execute `book.destroy!` in the test environment. I *need* to see exactly what's left behind. This is the only way I can ensure this crucial operation works the way I expect.

arguments.command:
bin/rails runner -e test '
tables = %w[
  users sessions sign_in_events accesses reading_marks
  books leaves edits pages sections pictures
  action_text_markdowns active_storage_attachments active_storage_blobs active_storage_variant_records
  leaf_search_index
]
counts_before = tables.index_with { |t| ApplicationRecord.connection.select_value("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM #{t}") }

alice = User.create!(name: "Alice Test", email_address: "alicetest@example.com", password: "secret123456")
book = Book.create!(title: "Alice Private Book", author: "Alice Test", everyone_access: false, creator: alice)
book.update_access(editors: [alice.id], readers: [])
book.cover.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "cover.webp", content_type: "image/webp")

page_leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: "v1 uniquealicepagev1"), title: "Alice Page")
page_leaf.page.body.uploads.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/white-rabbit.webp")), filename: "rabbit.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
page_leaf.page.save!
page_leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "v2 uniquealicepagev2" })

sec_leaf = book.press(Section.new(body: "s1 uniquealicesecv1"), title: "Alice Sec")
sec_leaf.edit(leafable_params: { body: "s2 uniquealicesecv2" })

pic_leaf = book.press(Picture.new(caption: "c1"), title: "Alice Pic")
pic_leaf.picture.image.attach(io: File.open(Rails.root.join("test/fixtures/files/reading.webp")), filename: "pic.webp", content_type: "image/webp")
pic_leaf.edit(leafable_params: { caption: "c2" })

trashed_leaf = book.press(Page.new(body: "trashed uniquealicetrashed"), title: "Trashed Page")
trashed_leaf.trashed!

ReadingMark.remember(page_leaf, user: alice)

puts "--- Destroying book ---"
Book.find(book.id).destroy!
alice.reading_marks.delete_all
alice.accesses.delete_all
alice.sessions.delete_all
alice.delete

counts_after = tables.index_with { |t| ApplicationRecord.connection.select_value("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM #{t}") }
tables.each do |t|
  diff = counts_after[t] - counts_before[t]
  puts "Table #{t}: before=#{counts_before[t]} after=#{counts_after[t]} LEFTOVER=#{diff}" if diff != 0
end
'

messages.thinking:
**Eureka! An Unexpected Oversight!**

Wow, *finally*! I've been chasing this down, and it looks like I've found it. That output is exactly what I was hoping to see! The `book.destroy!` call is leaving behind a whole slew of orphaned records. The tables are all showing leftovers - pages, sections, pictures, markdown, attachments, and blobs!

I'm seeing six tables left over: the pages, sections, and pictures are likely from the `has_many :edits, dependent: :delete_all` association in `Leaf::Editable`. The orphaned `action_text_markdowns` are really interesting—it looks like the duplication logic missed copying the `markdown_body`, and its attachments, during the `leaf.edit` process. Then, there are the `active_storage_attachments`, which seems like `Page` v1 has uploads attachment on `markdown_body` and `Picture` v1 has an image attachment. 

But wait, the `active_storage_blobs` are the biggest puzzle. Three blobs are left over! Why are *those* not being cleared out? It's hitting me, *now*! `Book#cover`, `Picture#image`, and `ActionText::Markdown#uploads` are using `purge_later`! Which means the `ActiveStorage::PurgeJob` is being enqueued, but it's not purging immediately when using the `:async` or `:test` adapter. And then there's the `dependent: :destroy` issue... ActiveStorage's `has_many_attached` doesn't *really* allow it! If you pass `dependent: :destroy`, it actually *disables* purging!! 

This is huge! We've got a potential leak that's been hiding in our test environment, and I need to confirm this thoroughly. First, let me get a clean test database and investigate. The focus is on ActiveStorage and the dependent relationships, particularly with `Leaf::Searchable` and `Leaf::Editable` and, of course, how that affects those blobs!

#   User.first.avatars.with_all_variant_records

  after_upload :analyze_blob_later
  after_upload :create_variants

First, the core of the issue: We're making a change that truly erases data, not just deactivates. The "Remove" button in the UI needs to *actually* remove the user and all associated data from the database. This includes their profile, any associated `SignInEvent` records, and, importantly, all the data we've added to support creating books and user's reading.

The code flow, in my mind, is this: When `user.destroy` (or `user.destroy!`) is called on a deactivated user, the system should:

*   Delete all the user's data from `users` table.
*   Delete `SignInEvent` entries associated with the user, even if they were under the *original* email address.
*   Erase the ActiveStorage blobs and files, including all attachments and variants and all associated records.
*   Cascade delete of all their `created_books` and destroy associated `leaf_search_index` entries.
*   Delete `reading_marks`.

Now, if a book was "shared with everyone" (`everyone_access: true`), it needs to remain accessible. However, we're making sure it no longer reflects the user as its creator. So, for these shared books, on user erasure:

*   The `creator_id` of the book is set to `nil`.
*   The `author` field of the book is updated to "Deleted author".

I'm thinking, "what happens if a user was previously 'removed' by being deactivated?" The existing system only sets the 'active' flag to false, scrambles the email address, and everything else stays. The new process needs to work on these "legacy deactivated" users, erasing them completely. This is key because that's our GDPR issue.

Let's carefully consider the UI implications. Previously, admins could only see active users on the `/users` page and click "Remove". I want to avoid breaking this, I'm thinking about whether we need to display deactivated users on the users list `/users`. Let's confirm:

messages.thinking:
**Transaction Shenanigans and FTS5 Integrity**

Okay, hold on a minute! I need to really dig into why `TestFixtures` in `Leaf::SearchableTest` worked. I remember Rails uses `begin_transaction(joinable: false)` in `TestFixtures`. That's key, I need to check if using `joinable: false` makes a difference. And, what about the possibility of someone calling `user.destroy!` inside an explicit `User.transaction do ... end` block? That could introduce some weirdness!

Now, the question is, why did `Leaf::Searchable` use `after_destroy_commit` instead of `after_destroy`? I need to look into this in `app/models/leaf/searchable.rb`:

module Leaf::Searchable
  extend ActiveSupport::Concern

Right, because in SQLite, `leaf_search_index` is a FTS5 virtual table *in the same database*! That's crucial. FTS5 tables *are* transactional. They participate in SQLite transactions and roll back on `ROLLBACK`.

But if we used `after_destroy_commit :remove_from_search_index` (without the `if: :searchable?` condition), here's what happens:

*   Outside an outer transaction (and that includes the Rails test transaction with `joinable: false`), when `user.destroy!` finishes its `User#destroy` transaction, the `after_destroy_commit` callback fires *immediately*!

*   What's the difference between `after_destroy` vs `after_destroy_commit`?
    *   If `after_destroy` runs *inside* the transaction:
        1.  Even *before* the outer transaction commits, the `leaf_search_index` table ALREADY has the row deleted!
        2.  If the transaction rolls back, SQLite rolls back the FTS5 `DELETE` automatically!
        3.  If the transaction commits, the FTS5 `DELETE` is committed *atomically* with the `leaves` `DELETE`. It's impossible to crash between `COMMIT` and `after_destroy_commit` leaving a stale search hit in SQLite!!

So, the real test is to verify that `DELETE FROM leaf_search_index` rolls back cleanly on `ROLLBACK` and commits cleanly on `COMMIT` within a transaction. Let's fire up `bin/rails runner -e test` and put this to the test!

**A Deep Dive into Rails Data Integrity**

Okay, so I just stumbled upon something significant in how we're handling creator associations in Rails, and it's got me thinking about potential pitfalls. I see that using `belongs_to :creator, default: -> { Current.user }` is essentially shorthand for a `before_validation` callback, specifically `before_validation { self.creator ||= Current.user }`. The problem is that it *doesn't* scope itself to `:create` as we expect, and this has some pretty serious implications.

Looking at the `Book::Authorship` module, it's immediately clear that scoping the default creator assignment to `:create` using `before_validation :set_default_creator, on: :create` is a much cleaner, more robust, and less error-prone approach. It provides much clearer behavior:

*   On *creation*, the `creator` is set to `Current.user` *only* if no creator is explicitly provided.
*   On *updates*, it *doesn't* interfere with our intended update logic. The `creator_id` isn't hijacked, even when explicitly set to `nil`, as it should be.

The implications are huge. The original approach could have led to a critical data integrity issue where an admin, by performing a "DELETE" action on a user, would silently corrupt data. The `creator_id` on books, intended to be `nil`, would get set to the admin’s ID during updates, which is the wrong behavior. This can lead to all sorts of issues when querying and displaying this data.

The module also prevents another important error in updating: that of resetting a book's creator to the current user even if it had a nil value.

This realization prompted me to check more potential vulnerabilities. We need to be very thorough.

Now, I'm thinking about edge cases. Specifically, what happens when an `everyone_access: true` book is retained, edited, updated, etc., after its creator is deleted?

Let's break down the implications:

1.  `book.creator` is `nil`. Good.
2.  `book.author` becomes `"Deleted author"`. Good.
3.  `book.everyone_access` remains `true`. Perfect.
4.  Alice's `Access` row is destroyed, but other users retain their `Access` rows. This is as we expected.
    -   What if Alice was the *only* editor on that book? Can admins still edit it? *Yes*, the `editable?` method correctly grants admins edit access, and other users have read access.
    -   How does the system display this data in the views after deletion? For example, what is shown when visiting:
        -   `BooksController#index`: `@books = Book.accessable_or_published.ordered` renders `_book.html.erb`, which shows `book.title` and `book.author` (`"Deleted author"`). This looks fine, but needs testing.
        -   `BooksController#show`: `@leaves = @book.leaves.active.with_leafables.positioned` renders `show.html.erb` (or `show.md.erb`), showing `@book.title`, `@book.subtitle`, `@book.author` (`"Deleted author"`). This also seems correct.
        -   `LeafablesController#show`: renders `leafables/show.html.erb` and `leafables/show.md.erb`. We should really read these files carefully to be sure.

I'm now going to go look at these view files (`app/views/leafables/show.html.erb`, `app/views/leafables/show.md.erb`, and `app/views/pages/edits/show.html.erb`) to ensure the correct values are being displayed and that there are no hidden interactions I need to know about. This is the only way to be completely sure.

**Eradicating User Data: A Deep Dive**

Okay, so the directive is clear: no trace, *nothing* left behind. I've gone over the code with a fine-tooth comb, and here's my understanding of how we achieve complete data erasure when a user is destroyed.

First, the attachments. We're only dealing with `Book#cover`, `Picture#image`, and `ActionText::Markdown#uploads`. The current `before_destroy` approach for books and related concerns could leave gaps. When we call `.purge`, we must make sure all records and the disk data are removed, even in the event of an outer transaction. It looks like the right approach will be to run the `purge_unattached_blobs` *after* the association is deleted. This allows `blob.attachments.none?` to return `true` immediately after the attachment is destroyed.

Now, the core of this operation. The `Purgeable` concern is key. It's a tiny, elegant solution that ensures, regardless of how a `Book`, `Picture`, or `ActionText::Markdown` is destroyed, all associated `ActiveStorage` entries and files on disk are obliterated, *provided* the file isn't still linked to something else. This happens *immediately* after the `ActiveStorage::Attachment` rows are destroyed. This prevents any stale data or orphaned files. This has to be tested, to make sure that the variant records are deleted and files purged in all cases.

Next, we look at the databases. We have 18 tables to worry about. We delete the `users` row, the `sessions`, `sign_in_events`, `accesses`, `reading_marks`, `books`, `leaves`, `edits`, `pages`, `sections`, `pictures`, `action_text_markdowns`, `active_storage_attachments`, `active_storage_variant_records`, `active_storage_blobs`, and the `leaf_search_index` rows. For shared books, we handle `creator_id` set to `nil` and `author` set to `"Deleted author"`.

I've also looked at `ActionCable`, `Turbo::StreamsChannel`, cache, cookies, and signed IDs. Signed transfers will return `nil`. Session cookies get deleted, logging users out. Cached HTML for a book is invalidated when `updated_at` changes.

Now, a couple of tricky edge cases. I needed to ensure that for shared books, we properly re-attribute the author as `"Deleted author"` even if `creator_id` is already `nil` or the author fields are empty. Books created before the migration are fine, because `creator_id` can be nullable. `everyone_access` is also safe because we update active user accesses. If a private book shares editor/reader access, those access rows are deleted, and everything else associated with that private book is deleted with `dependent: :destroy`. Also, deactivating a user multiple times works too, due to the way that email deactivation works, using a UUID.

I also checked the `UsersController`. Only active users are modified or destroyed. When a user is destroyed, their `ActiveRecord` record is erased and the active/non-active user count changes, so that the "erasure" does not result in errors or incorrect counts. The `users` row will be gone.

To finalize this approach, I need a robust reproduction script, verifying that *every* case is handled completely, right down to the last `ActiveStorage::Blob`.

**Alright, let's break this down.** The core issue here is ensuring that when a user's data is erased (as per GDPR), we *completely* remove all associated files from disk, but without breaking the test suite (specifically the `positionable_test.rb` test fixture). The previous implementation of `Picture#destroy` calling `blob.purge` globally was a disaster waiting to happen, potentially deleting files needed by other tests!

My solution is to introduce a *controlled* purge:

1.  **Delayed Purge for Most Cases:** Active Storage's default `dependent: :purge_later` on `has_many_attached` associations is PERFECT in most scenarios (like destroying a leaf or a book via the standard rails mechanism, as this enqueues jobs via ActiveStorage's standard mechanism without breaking existing tests). This handles the removal *most* of the time.
2.  **Synchronous, Specific Purge for User Erasure:** When a *user's* data is erased, we want to nuke all their private content *immediately*. Specifically, we add an `erase` method to `Book`, (or `Book::Authorship` / `Book`, or we could add the logic inline to `User::Authoring`) that iterates *synchronously* over all associated `ActiveStorage::Blob`s (cover, pictures, markdown uploads, and variants - both current, historical *and* trashed) and *only* calls `blob.purge` on those *unattached* to other records. This avoids any race conditions and ensures everything is gone *immediately*. Crucially, the code to find these blobs leverages associations to make it blazing fast. This *synchronous* approach ensures that the database and files are always in sync when a user is deleted.
3.  **Careful File Operations:** `ActiveStorage::Blob#delete` (via `DiskService#delete`) gracefully handles missing files, which handles any edge cases like a file already being deleted.

Let's check the new code:

*   The key change is in `User::Authoring` (called when `user.destroy` / `user.destroy!` / `DELETE /users/:id` is called): Before deleting the `book`, we call `book.erase`
    *   `Book#erase` gathers a list of *all* associated `ActiveStorage::Blob` ids (primary and derivative), and *only* purges the blobs *not* attached to other records. This ensures no shared files are accidentally erased, while all *private* files are deleted synchronously.
*   The `collect_attachment_blob_ids` method is incredibly efficient. It uses a series of optimized queries to gather the relevant blob IDs, combining `ActiveStorage::Attachment` records for the book itself, pictures (both active and historical), and markdown uploads (both active and historical).
*   The logic also needs a subtle tweak in `lib/rails_ext/action_text_markdown.rb`: we change `dependent: :destroy` to no `dependent:` flag (because we've changed its behaviour above).

With these changes, a user's private data is wiped clean and synchronous, while any shared data remains safe and available. The test suite, thanks to the controlled synchronous purge, is bulletproof. The code is clean, efficient, and ensures that we meet GDPR requirements *without* introducing regressions. I've also double-checked the files that will be modified for safety. Finally, I'll be sure to verify that deleting books, leaves, and other data *without* a user erasure continues to work as expected.

That includes *all* associated leaf data too; I'm talking leaves, edits, pages, sections, pictures, markdown, attachments, variant records, and that crucial `leaf_search_index` data. I'm going to verify that after deletion, the search index is *completely* clean, no lingering hits or rows.

For *shared* books, it's a bit more nuanced. If the user created a book with `everyone_access: true`, deletion has to: preserve the book, set the `creator` to `nil` (even if `Current.user` is an admin!), and change the `author` field to `"Deleted author"`.  Crucially, the user's `Access` and `ReadingMark` rows on that book have to be removed, but other users' access should remain unaffected. If the user only had `Access` or `ReadingMark`s on a book created by *someone else*, that book should be untouched.

Now, for those previously deactivated users, the destruction must be thorough. If they've been deactivated, their deletion needs to wipe everything – including any `SignInEvent` rows tied to their *original* sign-in email address, not just the deactivated one.

Moving to `test/controllers/users_controller_test.rb`, I need to nail down the controller behavior. The `destroy` action has to accurately reduce the `User.count` by one. Verify this, and verify that the deleted user is *actually* gone (using `User.find_by(id: ...)`). Confirm that all private books and search hits are obliterated. Shared books must get anonymized – `"Deleted author"`, `creator_id: nil` – and then verify that those books still render the `"Deleted author"` string, not the user's name, on the relevant paths. And of course, the `destroy` action must also handle those deactivated users properly, erasing their `User` row *and* their sign-in events under their *original* email address.

Finally, the `index` action should show deactivated users to admins, complete with a "Remove" button and working UI, while hiding them from non-admins.

Finally in `test/models/leaf/editable_test.rb` and `test/models/leaf/searchable_test.rb`, I'll have to deal with the cascading effects of leaf destruction. When a leaf is destroyed, along with any associated edits (revisions, trashed, etc), all its related content must be destroyed: pages, sections, pictures, and any markdown content. The leaf's entry in the `leaf_search_index` has to be removed, even if the leaf is marked as "trashed" or if the searchable content happens to be `nil`.

With this testing plan in place, I feel confident we can solidify the destruction logic. Let's add these tests right now and then run the whole test suite along with RuboCop for good measure.

3. **Shared Book Retention & Anonymization (`Book::Authorship`)**:
   - Preserved books created by the user that are shared with everyone (`everyone_access: true`), clearing `creator` (`nil`, scoped `set_default_creator` to `on: :create` so the acting administrator does not become the creator) and setting the `author` byline to `"Deleted author"`.
